summary: For children aged 5–6, build-and-test a shade structure that reduces the warming effect of sunlight on a spot (aligned to NGSS K-PS3-2 engineering design). The central learning is a hands-on design loop: choose materials, build a cover (umbrella/canopy/tent/parasol), position it between the sun and a target spot, then test by comparing the shaded spot with an unshaded one at the same time. Key insight: blocking the sunlight (opacity and position), not just covering, is what keeps the area cooler. Check which cover works by looking at the shadow or bright patch on the ground — never by looking toward the sun. An on-screen design bench and reference/check activities support the loop and fair-comparison logic, but the real outdoor build-and-test is what the standard requires.
misconceptions: 'Any cover works the same' — a see-through or holey cover still lets the sun warm the area; blocking the sunlight is what matters (opacity/coverage).
'Shade makes cold' — carried from the prior topic; the structure doesn't make cold, it stops the sun reaching and warming the area.
Thinking the structure must be big or tall rather than POSITIONED to block the sun's path to the area.
Treating the first build as finished — missing that testing and improving (iteration) is the task.
Judging success by looks ('it's a nice tent') rather than by the evidence (is the shaded spot actually cooler than the sunny one?).

activities.title: Build, position and test a real shade
steps: Start from a real problem the child cares about: 'the slide / sandpit / our toy gets too hot in the sun — can you build something to keep it cool?'

Offer a kit — cloths, card, sticks, pegs — and ask the child to choose a material and build a cover (umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol) over a target spot (a thermometer, a toy, or something to keep cool such as a chocolate or ice cube on the ground).
Have the child place the cover so it sits BETWEEN the sun and the spot; look at the ground and move the cover until the target spot is in the cover's shadow instead of bright sunlight.

Set up a fair comparison: two of the same kind of spot that start out alike, one shaded by the structure and one left in the sun, then check both after the same time has passed, by careful feel or with a relative thermometer.
Improve one thing and re-test (bigger? thicker/more opaque? angled to block the sun's path?), then judge success from the evidence: is the shaded spot cooler than the sunny one?
activities.insight: A shade works by getting between the sun and the area and blocking the sunlight; you can tell it worked because the shaded spot is cooler than a matching sunny spot checked at the same time, not because it looks nice.

activities.title: On-screen shade-design bench (companion for the design loop)
steps: Show a toy on a sunny slide (or a spot on a play area) and a kit of covers — cloth, open net, card — that the child can drag over the spot, resize and position relative to the sun.

Run a 'sun test' over time with two probes that start alike, one covered and one uncovered: across the test the uncovered spot keeps warming (warm face) while the covered spot stays cooler (cool face), so the difference grows over elapsed time rather than appearing instantly.
Use a 'change one thing' control and a persistent results strip that keeps each test's hit/miss mark on screen, so a pre-reader can read their own evidence and judge 'did it work?'.

Have the child try an open see-through net first and watch it still let light reach the spot so the spot keeps warming, then swap to a solid opaque cloth and re-test over the same time to see the covered spot stay cooler (note a tight weave may only partly reduce warming).

Keep all prompts picture + audio and all temperature language relative (warmer/cooler, no degrees); read which build worked from the shadow under the cover and the two probes, not by looking toward the sun.
activities.insight: Blocking the sun's light — not merely covering — is what keeps the spot cooler, and the structure must sit between the sun and the area; you confirm it by comparing covered and uncovered probes over the same time across repeated tests.

activities.title: Explore real shade exemplars (reference)
steps: Share a tappable or picture scene of real shade structures — umbrella, tent, canopy, sun-sail — and reveal the cooler area beneath each with 'this blocks the sun so it's cooler underneath' in picture + audio.
Ask the child to point out where each structure sits relative to the sun and which patch of ground it keeps in shadow.
Connect to the prior idea that the sun warms the area: because the sun warms the ground, a structure helps by getting between the sun and the spot.
activities.insight: Real shade structures all work in the same way — they get between the sun and the ground to block the light and cast a shadow — so position and coverage matter, not just size.

activities.title: Quick check — which cover keeps it coolest? (recognition)
steps: Pose a picture + audio question such as 'which shade keeps it coolest?' or 'is the spot under the umbrella warmer or cooler?' comparing a see-through cover with a solid one.
Ask the child to match a shade structure to the cooler shaded area beneath it, looking at which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground.
Keep temperature language relative (warmer/cooler) and provide adult/audio support for pre-readers.
activities.insight: A solid, well-positioned cover casts a dark shadow and keeps the spot cooler than a see-through or poorly placed one.

checkQuestion: Here are cloth, card, sticks and pegs. Make something that will keep this spot of ground (with a thermometer or toy on it) cooler in the sunshine. Set it up, then show me how you'll check whether it worked. [Watch: does the child place the cover BETWEEN the sun and the spot, block the light fully, and compare the shaded spot with a sunny one to test?]
checkAnswer: Builds a cover that physically blocks the sunlight from reaching the spot — positioned between the sun and the target, opaque enough to cast real shade — then tests by comparing the temperature or feel of the shaded spot against an unshaded spot, judging it worked if the shaded one is cooler.
